kp.k: Competence may eventually require AI use
kp.d: Leonard and McCormack argue that legal ethics discussions should expand beyond risks of AI use to possible risks of non-use. McCormack suggests that competent representation might require AI when it performs relevant tasks better than lawyers alone. This is a proposed evolution of professional obligations, not a reported ruling establishing a general duty to use AI.
qs: But you might have to use it to provide competent representation once the technology can do things that you simply can’t do as well.
almost all of the conversation around ethics has been focused on the ethical risks involved in using AI—hallucinations and biases.

kp.k: Verdict headlines overstate AI's demonstrated contribution
kp.d: McCormack describes two Georgia medical malpractice cases with verdicts of $25 million and $7.2 million. She cautions that AI-focused headlines overstate its role: lawyers used ChatGPT to assist case presentation and preparation, rather than submitting AI-written documents to court. The accounts illustrate uses of AI, without establishing that AI caused the outcomes.
qs: One—both were med mal cases. And both were in Georgia—personal injury practices in Georgia. One where there was a $25 million verdict, and one where there was a $7.2 million verdict.
But I think it overstated the role of AI in each of them.
They weren’t using it for researching or presenting AI-written documents to a court, which seems to be where everybody has the most concern, but rather to help them present their case.

kp.k: AI assists jury communication and expert preparation
kp.d: According to McCormack, the lawyer in the $25 million case used ChatGPT to develop ways of explaining an injury to jurors. In the other case, she reports, with the qualification 'I believe he said,' that AI-assisted preparation located a paper contradicting an opposing expert's testimony. She recommends supplementing ordinary preparation with targeted exploration of expert reports and other available material.
qs: So in the $25 million case, the lawyer used ChatGPT to help her think about how to talk about the particular injury to a jury.
I believe he said they were even able to find a paper where one of the experts on the other side had said not-X when he was testifying to X.
You’d do all the things you normally do, I think.

kp.k: Confidentiality and human verification remain essential
kp.d: McCormack pairs her argument for adoption with explicit safeguards: protect confidential information and check AI output because the system may answer despite uncertainty. Her position is augmentation under lawyer oversight, not direct reliance on unchecked output.
qs: Yes, you want to be really careful about what you do with any confidential information.
And you want to check the technology’s work, because it will give you an answer even when it’s not sure.
I hope more lawyers start to think about these tools as augmenters of their abilities.

kp.k: Client interests should guide ethical adoption
kp.d: Leonard criticizes the profession as insufficiently client- and public-centered. She conjectures that most clients would want lawyers to use powerful tools with safety guardrails, and welcomes ABA guidance and discussion of informed consent. This is her normative argument and expectation about client preferences, not survey evidence or a detailed account of a rule.
qs: we’re not client-centered enough, not public-centered enough, and we’re very lawyer and judge-centric.
would you like us to use it with safety guardrails in place? I don’t know many people who would say no.
I think it’s good that the ABA guidance came out and there’s discussion about having informed consent with your clients.

kp.k: Cost pressures combine with quality-based adoption arguments
kp.d: McCormack reports that in-house counsel have framed AI-enabled cost reductions as an ethical obligation and says the ABA formal opinion flagged fees. She also identifies competitive pressure when neighboring providers offer equivalent services more cheaply. Her additional argument is that adoption can improve quality, not merely reduce cost; no specific fee rule, savings measurement or pricing arrangement is supplied.
qs: And we’ve heard from in-house counsel who say, “If you can do the work with the help of this technology at a fraction of the cost, there’s an ethical rule that says you have to do that.”
If my neighbor’s figuring it out and can offer the same services significantly cheaper, if I want to continue to compete, I’m going to have to use it.
It’s not only that you can do it and save money—but that’s true here as well—it’s that you can do it better.

kp.k: Resource-constrained litigators may gain stronger capabilities
kp.d: Drawing on her experience relying on volunteer experts, McCormack sees substantial potential for small firms, solo practitioners and post-conviction Innocence Clinic practices without large litigation budgets. She speculates that traditional expenditure on experts or countering experts may become less necessary. Leonard adds that enhanced research and argument preparation could help plaintiffs' lawyers compete against much larger firms, while noting that the two cases did not specifically involve enormous opposing firms.
qs: There’s a tremendous upside for lawyers who are working on really important cases but don’t have big budgets—whether they’re at small firms, in solo practice, or in post-conviction Innocence Clinic practices—where they really don’t have the budgets for experts or to counter experts that traditionally you needed. I’m not sure you do anymore.
Not that they were enormous firms on the other side in these two specific cases.

But you can see how going up against a behemoth firm—if you’re able to source some of that research or shape your closing argument in a way that you wouldn’t have otherwise—it just gives you such a leg up.

kp.k: Accuracy and research superiority claims have limited detail
kp.d: Leonard cites a previously discussed VALS benchmarking study as support for the claim that AI is increasingly as accurate as humans at producing new content, but supplies no methods, sample sizes or performance figures here. McCormack separately asserts that current deep research capabilities exceed human research capabilities. These are, respectively, a reported interpretation of benchmarking and a speaker's broad assessment, rather than findings demonstrated within this transcript.
qs: But we’re starting to see data—and we talked about it on a recent podcast with the VALS benchmarking study—that AI is increasingly as accurate as we are at producing new content.
no matter how good we are at legal research or Google research or any other kind of research, we're no match for what the capabilities are that this technology has now.

kp.k: Everyday workflows illustrate conversational AI assistance
kp.d: Leonard recounts using ChatGPT voice mode to review a website with approximately 25 subpages, suggest clearer wording and compile page-by-page corrections. She describes substantial perceived time savings but provides no measured comparison. McCormack's photo-based identification and interactive nature tutoring anecdote likewise illustrates perceived usefulness rather than independently verified accuracy. These examples frame AI as an assistant that organizes feedback and offers suggestions under user direction.
qs: And it's a small website, but even for a small website, there's like 25 subpages that you click onto.
Can you take this and turn it into a bullet point list of page-by-page corrections?

It was like this interactive ChatGPT was walking me through the plants in the woods and teaching us about them.

kp.d: McCormack reports that Daniel Kokotajlo and AI Futures Project co-authors forecast AI potentially surpassing human intelligence by 2027 and changes within the decade exceeding those of the Industrial Revolution. She recalls that the scenario's timing was moved back a year. The hosts present this as scenario forecasting intended to stimulate discussion, not an established outcome, and attribute credibility to the authors' reported forecasting history and independence from AI labs.
qs: basically, it’s this very detailed scenario forecasting document that predicts the ways in which AI might evolve over the next few years.
he and his co-authors believe that AI could surpass human intelligence by 2027
within this decade, there will be enormous changes that exceed those of the Industrial Revolution.
And the point of the report wasn’t to be perfectly right about everything, but to raise awareness and start conversations.

kp.k: Forecast mechanisms include automation, rivalry and public backlash
kp.d: McCormack finds it intuitively plausible that AI surpassing humans at coding and supervising AI coders would accelerate progress. Leonard highlights the report's US–China rivalry scenario, research agents as a step toward superintelligence, and projected public backlash from job disruption. She reports a dashboard figure of around 1% currently seeing AI as a major problem rising to 20% in two years; this is presented within the forecasting discussion, not as an observed change. Leonard connects research agents to law's research-intensive work.
qs: once AI is better than humans at coding, it can supervise other AI coders. And at that point, progress accelerates rapidly.
one was this idea of an escalating war for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China.
they show a data point where currently around 1% of the public sees AI as a major problem. But in two years, when they predict superintelligence to emerge, that number jumps to 20%.
they view research agents as one of the key steps toward superintelligence. That feels squarely in the legal wheelhouse.

kp.k: Institutional barriers may delay adoption despite technical progress
kp.d: McCormack qualifies the rapid-growth scenario by distinguishing technological progress from full adoption, which legal, societal and human bottlenecks could slow. Leonard contrasts forecasts of superhuman capability in two to three years with lawyers who are not yet discussing AI. Their recommendation is awareness and practical experimentation, supported by concrete examples lawyers can relate to.
qs: Even if the forecasting is right, there are still lots of bottlenecks—legal, societal, human—that could slow full adoption.
there are people who believe that in two to three years, this technology will be superhuman. It’s wild to think about that when so many lawyers still aren’t talking about AI at all.
These two specific examples are so great because they are concrete. And lawyers will be able to relate to them right away.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack argue that AI can improve legal representation, not merely reduce its cost, and that competent practice may consequently require its use.
pts.d: McCormack identifies two concrete litigation applications: helping a lawyer explain an injury persuasively to a jury and helping prepare to counter opposing expert testimony, including locating an expert's inconsistent published statement. She claims that current deep-research capabilities exceed lawyers' unaided research capabilities. Leonard invokes benchmarking to claim that AI is increasingly as accurate as humans at producing new content. Both frame these capabilities as augmentation of lawyers, rather than autonomous representation. McCormack advances a conditional ethical argument: when available technology can improve representation in ways a lawyer cannot match unaided, not using it may become inconsistent with competent representation. Leonard similarly anticipates a shift toward treating an understanding of AI integration as an ethical requirement. These are the speakers' arguments and predictions, not a reported ruling establishing a general duty to use AI.

pts.k: McCormack predicts cost-based competitive pressure to adopt AI, while both speakers anticipate advantages for resource-constrained litigators.
pts.d: McCormack argues that firms will need AI to remain competitive when neighboring providers offer equivalent services substantially more cheaply. She distinguishes this cost argument from the additional claim that AI can improve work quality. Drawing on her litigation and clinical experience, she anticipates substantial benefits for small firms, solo lawyers and post-conviction innocence practices that cannot afford experts or the resources traditionally needed to counter them; she tentatively suggests those traditional resource requirements may diminish. Leonard argues that AI-assisted research and argument preparation can give plaintiffs' lawyers an advantage when facing much larger firms. Neither speaker quantifies savings, changes in market share or reductions in expert expenditure.

pts.k: As background rather than a legal-market forecast, the speakers relay AI 2027's predictions of rapid capability growth and social disruption, while identifying research agents as relevant to law.
pts.d: The forecast is attributed to Daniel Kokotajlo and his AI Futures Project co-authors, as described secondhand in the episode: AI could surpass human intelligence by 2027 and produce changes within the decade exceeding those of the Industrial Revolution. Leonard also reports the scenario's projected increase from around 1% to 20% of the public seeing AI as a major problem over two years, alongside job disruption and backlash. These are scenario claims, not employment or public-opinion findings established in this transcript. The credibility basis offered is the speakers' account of the authors' forecasting record, methodology and independence from a commercial lab; no underlying validation is reproduced. McCormack finds an acceleration mechanism involving AI supervising AI coders intuitively plausible. Leonard connects the report's emphasis on research agents to research-intensive legal work but does not supply a legal automation or displacement estimate. McCormack qualifies any capability forecast by noting that legal, societal and human bottlenecks could delay full adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The legal-service claims rest on two reported litigation examples, an unspecified benchmarking reference, professional experience and ethical reasoning.
pts.d: The principal examples are two unnamed Georgia medical-malpractice cases with reported verdicts of $25 million and $7.2 million. McCormack describes ChatGPT assistance with jury-facing injury explanations in the first and opposing-expert preparation in the second. She explicitly rejects attributing the verdicts themselves to AI. The transcript supplies neither case citations nor a comparison showing what would have happened without AI. Leonard references a previously discussed Vals AI benchmarking study but supplies no scores, tasks, sample sizes or methodological details here. McCormack's broader claims about research capability draw on the speakers' experience with deep research, while her resource-equalization argument draws on her jury-trial and Innocence Clinic experience. ABA guidance and a formal opinion are invoked as ethical context, without an opinion number or quoted rule text. McCormack separately reports an ethical cost-saving argument made by in-house counsel; that reported view should not be treated as an independently established legal obligation. Leonard's suggestion that clients would favor guarded AI use is a hypothetical judgment, not a client-survey finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The speakers describe litigation benefits as available now, but make ethical necessity conditional on capability, confidentiality safeguards and human verification.
pts.d: In this 2025 episode, the litigation applications and deep-research capabilities are presented as current. Leonard describes the potential ethical shift as occurring 'soon,' without a deadline; McCormack ties it to knowing that AI can improve representation and perform relevant work better than the lawyer alone. Their recommended use remains supervised: protect confidential information, check outputs and retain ordinary preparation rather than treating AI as an unchecked substitute. Leonard endorses discussion of informed client consent. McCormack initially distinguishes these examples from the legal research and AI-written court submissions that attract concern, although she also describes an expert-paper search in the second case; the distinction is principally between trial preparation and reliance on generated material submitted to a court. Their resource and competition claims are conditional on useful capabilities and competitors actually offering lower-cost equivalent services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed benefits primarily concern litigators and their clients, particularly those facing budget constraints or larger opponents; competitive pressure extends to legal-service providers more generally.
pts.d: Medical-malpractice and other plaintiffs' lawyers are presented as gaining help with explaining complex or emotionally difficult facts and challenging experts. Juries are the recipients of clearer case presentations. Small firms, solo practitioners and post-conviction innocence practices are identified as potential beneficiaries of capabilities previously constrained by expert and research budgets. Clients are expected to benefit from stronger representation and potentially lower fees, with Leonard suggesting that most would want AI used with safeguards. This is a predicted client preference, not measured evidence. In-house counsel appear as buyers pressing the cost argument, not as providers. Larger opposing firms are identified as a possible competitive reference point, but Leonard explicitly notes that the two examples did not necessarily involve enormous opposing firms. The discussion does not establish a measured reduction in unmet civil legal need or quantify profession-wide employment effects.
